title: Sharks Are Smarter — and Friendlier — Than You Think
paragraphs: Many people think of sharks as dangerous animals that live alone. However, new research shows that sharks may be smarter and more social than most people believe.

In 2026, scientists from the University of Exeter in the UK and the Fiji Shark Lab published a study about bull sharks. Bull sharks are large and strong, and many people think they are aggressive. The scientists studied 184 bull sharks for six years at a marine reserve in Fiji, in the Pacific Ocean.

The scientists found that the sharks did not just swim with any other shark. Instead, they chose to spend time with some sharks and avoided others. In other words, they had "friends." Adult sharks were the most social, and they often spent time with sharks of a similar size. Sometimes, two sharks swam side by side, or one shark followed another.

Natasha Marosi, who led the study, said that friendships may help sharks learn new skills, find food and avoid fights. Darren Croft, another scientist on the team, said that sharks "have relatively rich and complex social lives."

Other scientists also say that sharks can think and make decisions. For example, white sharks have been seen avoiding places where other dangerous animals are. Chris Lowe, a shark expert in California, said that understanding this can help people feel less afraid. Research has also shown that people who believe sharks can think and feel are more willing to protect them.
In fact, sharks bite people very rarely. According to the International Shark Attack File, there were only 105 shark bites on humans around the world in 2025.
